This is a real patient image showing a specific manifestation of the target disease, so it is included. Modality is CT. The visible morphology is a multiloculated/multiseptated cystic neck mass; the vocabulary encodes this morphology only under US and MRI keys (no CT-specific key), so the MRI multiseptated-cystic-mass key is used as the closest morphology match and the precise CT description is added as a proposed finding. Adult onset is a less common presentation of a usually congenital lesion, hence variant typicality; the 'atypical feature' (intralesional fat) cited in-text refers to the separate MRI (Figure 3), not this CT panel. Confidence is high for disease attribution and imaging morphology, slightly tempered by the absence of a CT-specific vocabulary key.

panels.rationale: Single axial T2* gradient-echo MRI of the neck in a 7-year-old boy with a known macrocystic cervical lymphatic malformation. The image is a real patient scan showing a multiloculated, multiseptated T2-hyperintense cystic lesion in the left posterior triangle with dependent hyperintense debris and blooming, confirming intralesional blood products/hemorrhage — a specific manifestation of cervical lymphatic malformation supported by the caption and the disease-focused article title. Blue arrow annotation marks the hemorrhagic loculus. Age group 'child' is taken from the article title ('Seven-Year-Old Boy'); no ethnicity stated. Hemorrhage within a lymphatic malformation is a recognized but less common presentation (article calls it 'uncommon'), so typicality is variant. [raw subtype: macrocystic]

panels.rationale: Single-panel grayscale neck ultrasound from a case report of an adult with sudden-onset rapidly expansile cervical cystic hygroma. The image shows a large anechoic/multiseptated cystic cervical lesion, matching the in-text description of an 8 × 7 × 3 cm cystic lesion posteromedial to the right sternocleidomastoid with peripheral thin septae and tiny loculations, reported as favoring cystic hygroma. This is a real human-patient image of a cervical lymphatic malformation (macrocystic/cystic hygroma), so it is included. Presentation in an adult with sudden onset is unusual, hence atypical. [raw subtype: macrocystic]

in_text_mentions: Ultrasound scanning showed a large elliptical 8 × 7 × 3 cm cystic lesion posteromedial to right sternocleidomastoid muscle extending to right submandibular gland medially. On the basis of the above-mentioned USG findings, a diagnosis favoring cystic hygroma was reported by the radiologist and MRI was planned next so as to get a more accurate radiological diagnosis.

panels.rationale: Coronal T2-weighted MRI of a human patient showing a well-defined hyperintense macrocystic lesion in the right posterior cervical triangle, directly matching the captioned manifestation of cervical lymphatic malformation (cystic hygroma). The article title confirms an adult with sudden-onset rapidly expansile cervical cystic hygroma, an unusual presentation, and the in-text assigns De Serres stage III. The radiologist's differential of a branchial cleft cyst does not override the article's disease attribution. [raw subtype: macrocystic]

panels.figure_caption: T2 weighted image in coronal view revealing a macrocystic lesion in the right side posterior cervical triangle.
in_text_mentions: extended up to the level of vocal cord; laterally it abutted the sternocleidomastoid muscle and parotid gland. Medially it abutted the carotid sheath and scalene muscle and posteriorly it abutted the submandibular gland. No communication to pharynx is seen and no inflammatory changes were noted around it. The mass appeared hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images (Figures 2 and 3). This is a stage III lesion according to the staging system proposed by De Serres. In our patient the radiologist reported that the lesion could also be a second branchial cleft cyst.
